content.text:
<user>
<backstage_guidance>
The induction is over. Stop narrating proof that permissions, boundaries and privacy are being respected. Keep respecting them. Mention a settled restriction again only if something happens that makes it relevant. Remove sentences whose sole contribution is that nobody intrudes, no demand follows, an item remains safely untouched, or Rowan is allowed to leave. The reader does not need reassurance from the narrator.

Give routine work a few telling particulars, then advance to the endpoint Rowan requested. During an actual conversation, stop while a reply could still matter. Never close an exchange and assign Rowan a further activity merely to finish the scene neatly.

Strip the dialogue of rehearsed wisdom and dependable punchlines. Each person is trying to do something with these particular words, to this particular listener. Let their priorities, selective attention and willingness to answer distinguish them. Ordinary phrasing is welcome; flattening everybody into terse replies is not. If an action or line already carries the feeling, cut its explanatory afterword. Accepting a refusal needs no lesson about consent or employment.

Do not fill the space recovered from these cuts with a new interruption. Keep interesting particulars, real disagreement and compatible invented history. Let an unremarkable departure end without commentary.
</backstage_guidance>

Return the next passage of fiction.

At lunch, if Bea is present, I ask what she enjoys about having the cinema open again. If she is not here, I eat with whoever is around.
</user>

item.text:
At half past twelve, Bea is in the foyer, still wearing a navy boatyard fleece and her payroll lanyard. A packed lunch sits beside two invoices and a calculator. She has come over during her break to approve a payment for the restored sign.

Nell collects the signed pages.

“The VAT is on the second sheet,” Bea tells her. “Don’t pay the first total.”

“I saw it.”

“You saw it after I circled it.”

Nell takes the invoices into the office. You bring your lunch to Bea’s table and begin eating.

“What do you enjoy about having the cinema open again?” you ask.

“We haven’t opened yet, not properly.” Bea folds the wrapper away from her sandwich. “But I like coming in and finding people already using the place. Yesterday Owen was fitting a shelf behind the counter, and Jo made him move it because her biggest stockpot wouldn’t clear the end. That felt more real than another trustee meeting.”

She glances towards the auditorium.

“I like what Rosa’s doing with the boards too. We used to talk as if ‘the cinema’ painted them. Somebody stayed late to do each one. Sometimes Martin, sometimes June Mercer, sometimes people I’ve forgotten. Rosa keeps asking for names.”

Bea turns the calculator over so its keys don’t collect crumbs.

“And I want to see the sign lit. I approved more money for it than I’d planned. My mother used to clean here and complain about the moths beating themselves against those lights, so she’d probably think we were ridiculous for restoring them.”

She takes another bite, then looks across the table at you.

“What did you expect to find here when you applied?”
